aged-brass.purpose: The one accent. Primary buttons, active nav and tab states, focus rings at low alpha, links. Deliberately rare: its scarcity is what makes it read as intentional rather than a default theme blue.

aged-brass-hover.purpose: Hover step for any accent-filled surface. The only state change a primary button makes — no scale, no transform.

ink-bg.purpose: App background, and the fill for input fields so a field reads as recessed from the card it sits on.

ink-card.purpose: Cards, stat tiles, table containers. One step lighter than the page — the primary depth cue, with shadow layered on as secondary.

ink-border.purpose: Structural borders: card edges, the table header rule, input outlines.

ink-border-lt.purpose: Internal borders: table row dividers, ghost button edges. Using the structural weight here makes a dense table read as a grid of boxes.

ink-sidebar.purpose: The sidebar column, theme-matched so it never reads as a fixed dark strip on a light preset.

text-primary.purpose: Primary text — a warm off-white, deliberately not pure white.

text-secondary.purpose: Secondary text: labels, metadata, table column headers. 6.70:1 on the card. Swapped with the tertiary tier in S620 — the values were always in the palette, just assigned the wrong way round, so every "quietest tier" hint rendered louder than every secondary label on Dark.

text-tertiary.purpose: The quietest tier: timestamps, disabled-adjacent copy, icon buttons at rest. 5.45:1. Both tiers cleared AA before and after the S620 swap — this was hierarchy, not accessibility, which is why no contrast audit caught it.

signal-success.purpose: Paid, approved, healthy stock, positive variance.

signal-danger.purpose: Overdue, rejected, negative variance, destructive actions.

signal-warning.purpose: Pending, low stock, needs-attention. Distinct from the accent, which is never a status color.

signal-categorical.purpose: The rationed 4th/5th categorical color, for when green/red/amber genuinely run out. Not a second accent.

chart-tick.purpose: Recharts axis tick, label and reference-line fill. CSS var() does not resolve inside SVG presentation attributes, so this one is a literal by necessity, not by drift.

toggle-knob.purpose: The sliding thumb inside a toggle switch. Always sits on a colored track, never directly on the page, so a fixed white holds contrast across all ten presets.

print-ink.purpose: Heading text and rule dividers on printed documents. Valid only inside a print-only component or an @media print block; never on screen.

print-text.purpose: Body copy needing more weight than a label. Valid only inside a print-only component or an @media print block; never on screen.

print-label.purpose: Secondary meta lines: dates, addresses, PAN/VAT. Valid only inside a print-only component or an @media print block; never on screen.

print-label-lt.purpose: Field labels and table body secondary text. Valid only inside a print-only component or an @media print block; never on screen.

print-notes.purpose: Notes and callout box text. Valid only inside a print-only component or an @media print block; never on screen.

print-muted.purpose: Uppercase section eyebrows, footer and index columns. Valid only inside a print-only component or an @media print block; never on screen.

print-faint.purpose: Generated-by footers; the least emphasis on the page. Valid only inside a print-only component or an @media print block; never on screen.

print-rule.purpose: Table header and footer rule lines. Valid only inside a print-only component or an @media print block; never on screen.

print-rule-strong.purpose: Bordered chips, e.g. a status pill outline. Valid only inside a print-only component or an @media print block; never on screen.

print-rule-lt.purpose: Notes-box border. Valid only inside a print-only component or an @media print block; never on screen.

print-rule-xlt.purpose: Table row divider. Valid only inside a print-only component or an @media print block; never on screen.

print-fill.purpose: Table header row background. Valid only inside a print-only component or an @media print block; never on screen.

signal-success-text.purpose: Success green used as text. Value shown is the DEFAULT (Dark) preset, where the variant deliberately resolves to its own base colour; Light declares its own darkened, hue-preserving value (#137538). Never resolve one of these to a literal — read the token.

signal-danger-text.purpose: Danger red used as text. Retuned S608: with amber-text it is the only pair of 120 searched that clears both deuteranopia and protanopia while every variant still holds 4.5:1. Value shown is the DEFAULT (Dark) preset, where the variant deliberately resolves to its own base colour; Light declares its own darkened, hue-preserving value (#8f2440). Never resolve one of these to a literal — read the token.

signal-warning-text.purpose: Warning amber used as text. Retuned S608 alongside danger-text — at the previous values the two sat at ΔE 3.2 under deuteranopia, i.e. one colour for ~6% of men. Value shown is the DEFAULT (Dark) preset, where the variant deliberately resolves to its own base colour; Light declares its own darkened, hue-preserving value (#a85200). Never resolve one of these to a literal — read the token.

signal-categorical-text.purpose: The rationed categorical purple used as text. Value shown is the DEFAULT (Dark) preset, where the variant deliberately resolves to its own base colour; Light declares its own darkened, hue-preserving value (#7c3aed). Never resolve one of these to a literal — read the token.

accent-ink.purpose: The accent used AS text (a link, an active nav item, a plan label) — not accent-text, which is the foreground that sits ON an accent fill. Value shown is the DEFAULT (Dark) preset, where the variant deliberately resolves to its own base colour; Light declares its own darkened, hue-preserving value (#7a561e). Never resolve one of these to a literal — read the token.

accent-text.purpose: The foreground that sits ON an accent-coloured fill — the label of a primary button, an active pill. Per preset: near-black on Dark, #241a08 on Light, (Latte/Rose Dawn/Solarized, retired S607, each needed a dark hue-match where plain white measured 2.84-3.68:1 and failed AA on every .btn-primary in the product — which is why this token exists at all.) Never hardcode a white or black here; reach for the token, then verify the token.

focus-ring.purpose: A TINT, not a focus indicator. It doubles as the active-state background for rail buttons, module tabs and sidebar links, so its alpha must stay low — measured alone on Rose Dawn (retired S607) it composited to 1.15:1, 2.6x below WCAG 2.2's 3:1 focus floor. Always paired with focus-outline; the ring by itself is decoration.

focus-outline.purpose: The actual keyboard-focus indicator (added S574): a 2px solid, resolved per preset as accentInk on light presets and the accent on dark. Every :focus-visible rule pairs this with the soft ring. A new focusable control that takes only the ring has no visible focus state on a light theme.

input-bg.purpose: The recessed ground behind a form control — equal to the page background on the dark presets, so a field reads as cut INTO the card rather than raised off it. Reached through .form-field input or .form-input; an input that gets neither renders as the browser's native white box (S593).

table-hover.purpose: The barely-there row-hover wash — 2-8% depending on preset. It is a pointer cue, not a selection state, and it must never be opaque enough to compete with the figures in the row. It is also what a sticky first column has to paint over, which is why .data-table--sticky-first sets an opaque card background.

guest-paper.purpose: Card and input ground on the public menu — the dish is read on this. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

guest-ground.purpose: Page behind the paper, one step back so a card can lift off it. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

guest-pine.purpose: The guest surface’s single accent: brand, price, category heading, active chip, CTA fill. Rationed exactly as Aged Brass is elsewhere. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

guest-pine-deep.purpose: Pressed/hover state of a pine fill. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

guest-ink.purpose: Dish names and body-strength text. 14.8:1. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

guest-sage.purpose: Dish descriptions. 6.1:1. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

guest-sage-lt.purpose: Nutrition tags, covers line, table name, smallest meta. 4.7:1 on ground, 5.1:1 on paper. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

guest-rule.purpose: Structural hairline; recedes on purpose. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

guest-control.purpose: Outlines a tappable control, clearing WCAG 1.4.11. 4.1:1. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

guest-veg.purpose: Veg mark — a market convention, not a palette choice. 4.3:1. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

guest-nonveg.purpose: Non-veg mark. 5.5:1. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

guest-success.purpose: Ready to serve. 5.5:1. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

guest-warn.purpose: Allergens — a safety line, so never faint. 5.1:1. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

guest-danger.purpose: Order dismissed, submit failed. 6.0:1. Guest menu only (.guest-menu); theme-independent by design — a public page cannot inherit whichever preset the scanning phone had saved.

wordmark.purpose: The "Crest" wordmark only — sidebar brand mark and the login screen. The one serif in an otherwise all-sans system, and it never appears on a second element.

body.purpose: Table cells, form values, and the default size for nearly everything a user reads.

label.purpose: Table column headers, stat card labels, section eyebrows. Uppercase at wide tracking, earning its place as a literal column header rather than a decorative kicker.

stat-value-lg.purpose: The single headline numeral on a dashboard hero tile.

stat-value.purpose: The numeral in a standard KPI card.

numeral.purpose: Inline figures that need to outweigh their surrounding body text.

page-title.purpose: The h1 at the top of a page.

section-heading.purpose: A major division inside a page.

rail-icon.purpose: Sidebar module-switcher icons in the collapsed rail.

card-heading.purpose: The title bar of a card or modal.

title.purpose: Card headings and section titles inside dense layouts.

meta.purpose: Timestamps, secondary row detail, helper text under a field.

micro.purpose: The smallest tier — badge text and uppercase micro-labels, at 700 weight so it stays legible at 10px.

chevron.purpose: Disclosure arrows in nav groups. Sized as an icon, not as text.

print-monospace.purpose: Thermal-printer receipts and KOTs, where fixed-width columns must stay aligned. Never inside the live app UI.

touch-input.purpose: Text-input only, scoped to .self-service. 16px is the threshold below which iOS Safari zooms the viewport on focus and never zooms back — not a taste step, and never usable as one. Pinning the viewport instead blocks pinch-zoom for everyone, which is why it is deliberately not done.

shadows.name: card-elevation
shadows.purpose: The default for .card / .stat-card, exposed as --theme-card-shadow. Generated per preset from that preset's own bg and text1 rather than a flat black, so a theme's color cast survives into its shadow. Dark presets get this rim-highlight-plus-deep-shadow form; light presets get a simpler 0 1px 2px + 0 10px 24px -8px pair tinted from their own ink.

shadows.name: floating-action
shadows.purpose: An element genuinely floating above the page: the Fab, the bottom-anchored guest cart button. One of only two shadows that still carry a distinct meaning now that card elevation is uniform policy.

shadows.name: live-pulse-ring
shadows.purpose: An animated breathing ring on something needing real-time attention (a new guest order, a live status dot), using the relevant signal color's own alpha. The second meaning-carrying shadow.

shadows.name: focus-ring
shadows.purpose: Themed focus indicator on inputs, selects and icon buttons. An alpha-blended version of the active preset's accent, so it changes hue with the theme instead of falling back to browser blue.

motion.name: motion-fast
motion.purpose: Duration for a state change in place: hover, active, focus, a nav item lighting up.

motion.name: ease-standard
motion.purpose: Paired with motion-fast. Symmetrical, because nothing is arriving or leaving.

motion.name: motion-slow
motion.purpose: Duration for something arriving that was not on screen: a modal panel, a stat pill resolving in.

motion.name: ease-entrance
motion.purpose: Paired with motion-slow. The near-flat tail reads as settling rather than stopping.

motion.name: button-transition
motion.purpose: Predates the token pair and is deliberately quicker — a button should feel immediate. No scale, no bounce, no elastic easing anywhere in the product.

motion.name: sidebar-collapse
motion.purpose: The one accepted layout-property animation. .sidebar-wrap is position:fixed so real space must be reserved; a transform-only version would slide the sidebar over the content instead of resizing the column. Fires only on a rare manual toggle.

motion.name: chart-series
motion.purpose: A second motion system that shares none of the CSS tokens on purpose. Recharts interpolates SVG attributes in JavaScript, so no CSS rule — including the prefers-reduced-motion guard — reaches a chart series; chartMotion.js is the only place that gate can live. It cannot express ease-entrance, since Recharts accepts only ease|ease-in|ease-out|ease-in-out|linear. Aligned with the shell on duration band, deliberately not on curve.

chartPalette.purpose: Chart series are fixed literal hex on purpose and are NOT theme tokens. Two independent reasons: CSS var() does not resolve inside SVG presentation attributes, and the five semantic tokens are five ROLES rather than five distinguishable hues — a constraint nothing measures for them, since they move to serve legibility and branding instead. Both concrete justifications this rule once cited have expired (accent/purple being one hex died with those presets in S607; Light's red/amber collapse was fixed in S609), which is the argument rather than a weakening of it. A hex appearing in a chart palette is not an accent-drift violation; the One Accent Rule governs UI chrome.
chartPalette.validatedAgainst: Re-measured 2026-08-24/S609 over the two surviving presets. Worst pair: normal vision ΔE 37.9, deuteranopia 15.8, protanopia 21.0 — all 28 pairs clear the ΔE 8 CVD floor on both axes. Slots 5 and 6 were changed to get there: #a78bfa → #8b5cf6 (blue/violet had sat at ΔE 0.4 under deuteranopia, i.e. two indistinguishable lines on any chart with five or more series) and #fb923c → #ea580c (gold/orange 4.2 under protanopia). TRITANOPIA is deliberately not satisfied — worst pair #f87171/#f472b6 at ΔE 0.9 — because separating on the blue-yellow axis fights separating on red-green, and tritanopia is ~0.01% and not sex-linked against ~8% of men for red-green. Acceptable only because these charts carry secondary encoding: paddingAngle gaps, on-slice percent labels, and name+value legends.

slots.name: Food Cost
slots.note: Gold. Kept identical across the cost pie, the FC% trend line and the Owner trend so one measure has one identity everywhere.

slots.name: Overheads / Prime
slots.note: Violet. Prime Cost draws it DASHED because it is the sum of the two lines above it, not a fifth peer.

slots.name: Net Margin
slots.note: Green — the one slice that stays semantic, because profit reading as good is not a coincidence worth breaking.

rules: A legend swatch must equal the series it labels. Darkening the swatch for contrast while the line keeps the series colour desynchronises them, which is worse than the contrast it fixes; the adjacent label text carries the readable contrast.
Prefer encoding a relationship over adding a hue. A metric's month-end projection repeats its metric's colour and is distinguished by a dash; a derived total reads as a dashed composite.
Red is not spent on a merely-categorical slice. On these dashboards red means "over threshold", so using it for "Overheads" or for the Prime Cost line made a neutral fact read as an alarm.
chartPalette.knownConstraint: The palette is tuned for the DARK card (#181c27), where every slot clears 4:1. On the Light card (#FCFAF6) six of eight fall below the WCAG 1.4.11 3:1 non-text floor — #22d3ee 1.81, #34d399 1.92, #c9a84c 2.29, #60a5fa 2.54, #f472b6 2.65, #f87171 2.77. Only #8b5cf6 (4.23) and #ea580c (3.56) clear it. This is survivable only because of the same secondary encoding above: the series are named and valued in the legend and labelled on-slice, so colour is reinforcement rather than the sole carrier. Fixing it properly means re-picking six hues that clear 3:1 on BOTH surfaces while still separating under deuteranopia and protanopia — a mid-tone palette with a different character from today's vivid-on-charcoal set. That is a design decision, not a correction.

components.name: Primary Button
components.description: The single accent-filled action on a screen. Foreground is always the paired accent-text token, never a hardcoded white or black.
components.html: <button class="ds-btn ds-btn-primary">Save Changes</button>

components.name: Ghost Button
components.description: The default button. Sits at page-background fill with a quiet internal border; hover steps the border to the accent — a restrained way of saying "this became interactive."
components.html: <button class="ds-btn ds-btn-ghost">Export Excel</button>

components.name: Danger Button
components.description: Destructive actions only — delete, void. Never used to mean "important". Red text on a tinted fill rather than a solid red fill, because --theme-red ranges from light to dark across the ten presets and no single foreground contrasts on all of them.
components.html: <button class="ds-btn ds-btn-danger">Void Bill</button>

components.name: Danger Button (Escalated)
components.description: One step up from the danger variant, for the single irreversible action inside a group of otherwise-recoverable destructive ones — Danger Zone's "Delete Client" beside Clear and Archive. Still a tint rather than a solid red fill, for the same reason the base variant is: --theme-red ranges light-to-dark across the ten presets and there is no --theme-red-text to pair with a fill. At most one per group, or the escalation means nothing.

components.name: Status Badge
components.description: Every semantic color renders as a ~10-12% alpha tint of itself with full-opacity text — never a solid fill with white text. That is what keeps a table calm when every row carries one.
components.html: Paid Pending Overdue Cancelled

components.name: Card
components.description: The standard surface. One tone lighter than the page as the primary depth cue, with a per-preset shadow layered on top. No gradient, no tint toward the accent.
components.html:
Period Summary

Net purchases, revenue and food cost for the open period.

components.name: Stat Card
components.description: A KPI tile: uppercase micro-label over a large numeral. Padding is 20px rather than the card default 24px — a label-and-numeral pair has no internal composition to breathe around, and a row of them reads better slightly denser.
components.html:
Food Cost %

components.name: Text Input
components.description: Label always sits above the field — a placeholder never stands in for a label. Focus steps the border to the accent and adds a themed 3px ring, not a browser-blue outline.

components.name: Tab Pill
components.description: The filter/sort control on nearly every list page. Active reads as selected, not pressed — accent text, accent border at 50% alpha, focus-ring token as fill. Deliberately at the standard 12px radius rather than full-pill, which is reserved for the sidebar module switcher.

components.name: Panel Tab (underline)
components.description: The second, distinct tab family: sections within one surface, typically a modal panel (ClientDrawer's eight), as opposed to Tab Pill's filter/sort controls which change what a single view shows. Bordered pill for a filter, underline for a section; never both in one row. A danger section keeps --theme-red in both states and takes its underline in red. The row wraps rather than overflowing — an overflowing tab bar silently hides its last tab, which is how ClientDrawer's Danger tab went missing for a release.

components.name: Data Table
components.description: The signature component — most of the product is built around it. 11px uppercase headers at wide tracking, 13px rows, light dividers, and a barely-there hover tint rather than a solid highlight. Actionable rows carry a right-aligned Actions column so a long queue never has to be scrolled to act on. Per S614: a cell holding two things is the one the auto layout collapses, so put nowrap on the cell (never a fixed width) and let .table-wrap scroll; row density is opted down through a table-level scoped class, never per cell.

components.name: Sidebar Nav Link
components.description: A nav row in the unified 240px sidebar column. Active state is accent text on the focus-ring tint at weight 600 — the same treatment the active tab pill uses, so "selected" reads identically everywhere.
components.html: PurchasesStock CountRecipes

components.name: Chart Expand Button
components.description: The only affordance saying a chart card opens. Sits in the quietest text tier, so it must acknowledge pointer and keyboard or it reads as an icon rather than a control. Holds a 24px minimum target (44px on coarse pointers) around a 12px glyph.

components.name: Stat Pill
components.description: A compact KPI callout for a ChartCard's expanded-only stat strip. The dot carries the SERIES colour (legitimately a chart hex); the value is text and defaults to text1, because a fill hex set as 13px/700 type measured about 1.9:1 on a light card.

components.name: Link-like Button
components.description: A table cell that navigates, or an inline action in a sentence. Reads as a link, behaves as a button — used where the row's identity IS the action (an outlet name that switches to that outlet), so the affordance sits on the name rather than in a trailing Actions column.

components.name: Chart Modal Panel
components.description: The expanded chart view. Keeps its own look (blurred backdrop, wide panel, legend inline in the header) but carries the full dialog contract: role/aria-modal/labelled title, initial focus on the panel rather than its Close button, a Tab trap, Escape, and focus restored to the trigger.

components.name: Report Error State
components.description: What a report renders INSTEAD of its KPI strip and table when a read fails. Deliberately not the empty state: 'nothing to show' and 'could not load' are different facts, and only one of them means the zeros on screen are real. Carries role="alert".

components.name: Standalone Input
components.description: An input OUTSIDE a .form-field wrapper — the natural shape whenever a field sits inline beside a button. Until .form-input existed (S593) the only themed rule was the descendant selector .form-field input, so these rendered as the browser's native white box: unmissable on dark presets, nearly invisible on light ones. Shares one declaration block with .form-field input so the two cannot drift.
components.html: <input class="ds-form-input" type="text" placeholder="or create a new group…" />

components.name: Table Totals Row
components.description: A table's tfoot. Until S594 .data-table tfoot had NO rule at all, so every totals row in the product was hand-styled at its call site and three report pages built in one week produced three different treatments. The row-hover tint is suppressed: a totals row is not a data row.

components.name: Field Caption (non-label)
components.description: A caption that looks like a <label> but is a <span>, used over a button group, a read-only figure, or a repeating row's column. A <label> referencing no labelable element announces a name the browser never binds to anything — worse than no label. .form-field .field-label carries the same typography, so the fix costs no visual change.

components.name: Sticky-First Matrix
components.description: Opt-in .data-table--sticky-first, for a wide matrix whose first column is the row label — Consolidated P&L with one column per outlet is the case it was built for. Without it, scrolling right to reach the last column scrolls the labels away and the reader matches numbers to remembered row order. The sticky cell needs an opaque background or the scrolling columns show through underneath.

components.name: Row Disclosure Button
components.description: The control that expands a table row's detail. It lives INSIDE a <td> so the <tr> keeps its implicit row role and its cells keep their column-header associations. The row's own onClick still toggles for mouse users; this button stops propagation so the two cannot cancel each other out.

narrative.overview:
Crest Suite is operated, not visited. An owner is checking margin between service rushes; an accountant is reconciling TDS figures before a filing deadline. Neither has time for the interface to perform. The system is built around legibility under pressure: dense tables that stay scannable, a single restrained accent, and status communicated through color and position rather than decoration.

This deliberately rejects two things named in PRODUCT.md: the dated, hierarchy-less density of legacy Nepali ERP software, and the templated purple-gradient look of generic AI-generated SaaS. The system solves density the same problem legacy ERPs were trying to solve, but with real typographic hierarchy, a single accent used sparingly, and consistent spacing instead of cramming.

The product runs across two interchangeable theme presets — Dark (charcoal-and-gold, the shipped default) and Light (warm white, the same design in a light scheme). Eight others (Tokyo Night, Dracula, Nord, Catppuccin, Latte, Rosé Dawn, Solarized, Bright) were retired on 2026-08-24/S607: every theme is an independent surface needing re-verification for every signal colour, badge and focus style, and a measured audit found 30 contrast failures concentrated in the four dark presets nobody had checked. Dark and Light both measured clean, and they are the pair system mode resolves between for the employee app — so they are also the two that cannot be removed. Both are built from the same token set. Every rule is written against the default preset's values, but the relationships between tokens hold across all ten, even where the literal shape values (radius, shadow) no longer do.
keyCharacteristics: Depth comes primarily from a one-step background-lightness shift, with a per-preset shadow as a secondary cue (added 2026-07-12 — see Elevation; previously flat-only, see that section's history note)
One accent color per screen, applied sparingly (buttons, active states, focus rings) never as a wash — no exceptions remain (Bright carried the only scoped one; retired with that preset in S607)
A serif wordmark is the one deliberate ornamental choice in an otherwise all-sans, all-functional system

Status (paid / pending / overdue, veg / non-veg, stock health) is color-coded consistently: green success, red danger, amber caution, gray neutral, with a rationed 4th color (purple) reserved for a genuine fourth or fifth category when green/red/amber aren't enough

rules.name: The One Accent Rule
rules.body: Aged Brass (or the active preset's own accent) is the only non-semantic color on any screen. If a second "brand" color shows up anywhere outside the rationed purple exception, it's a mistake, not a design choice. Seven separate recurrences of an undocumented indigo (#60a5fa / #818cf8 / a drifted #8b5cf6 var() fallback) have been found and fixed across AdminClients.js, SuiteGate.js, AuditLog.js, AdminDashboardOverview.jsx, HolidayCalendar.jsx, MenuEngineering.js and Login.css — grep for those literals before shipping any new categorical badge or pill, and check the fallback halves of var() calls, not just standalone literals.

rules.name: The Accent-Text Pairing Rule
rules.body: Any element with an accent-colored background uses the theme's paired accent-text token for its foreground, never a hardcoded white or black. Because the accent changes per preset, a hardcoded foreground will silently fail contrast on at least one of the ten. Shipped and fixed twice — treat any hardcoded #000/#fff sitting next to var(--theme-accent) as a near-certain instance on sight.

rules.name: The One Serif Rule
rules.body: Georgia appears exactly once per screen (the wordmark, if visible at all). It is never used for a heading, a callout, or emphasis — that would dilute it from signature to affectation.

rules.name: The Auto-Fit-First Rule
rules.body: Reach for repeat(auto-fit, minmax(<floor>, 1fr)) before declaring a column count. A fixed count is a claim that the grouping matters at every width; if it doesn't, the fixed count is just a media query you now have to maintain.

rules.name: Shadow tells you what surface you're on, not that a page is "polished"
rules.body: Card elevation is uniform policy (every preset, every card), so it no longer functions as a special signal the way the floating-action and live-pulse shadows still do. Don't invent a third meaning for it. If something needs to stand out, that's a job for the accent color or position.

rules.name: The Proportional Corner Rule
rules.body: If a new element needs a radius, pick the step by asking how big the box is, not how important it is. An "important" card does not get a larger corner; it gets the accent color or a better position.

rules.name: Badges are alpha-tint, never solid fill
rules.body: Each semantic color renders as a ~10-12% alpha tint of itself as background with full-opacity text. A solid signal fill needs a paired foreground token and only --theme-accent has one, so red/amber/green must use the tint pattern. This keeps a table full of status badges calm even when every row has one.

rules.name: Row actions belong on the row
rules.body: A table whose rows can be acted on carries a right-aligned Actions column of ghost buttons tinted with the semantic color of what they do. Putting the only actions in a detail panel below the table means the distance between the row you decided about and the button that acts on it grows with the list.

rules.name: Every animation must be switch-off-able by prefers-reduced-motion, which means it cannot be an inline style
rules.body: Inline style={{ animation }} beats any stylesheet rule, so a media query cannot reach it — the animation is then unconditional for every user regardless of their OS preference. Put animations in a class; put the class in the reduced-motion block at the foot of its section in Layout.css.

rules.name: Recharts is a second motion system that shares none of these tokens, on purpose
rules.body: It interpolates SVG attributes in JavaScript, so no CSS rule — including the reduced-motion guard — reaches a chart series. Every series goes through src/shared/chartMotion.js, the only place that gate can live. It cannot use ease-entrance: Recharts accepts only ease|ease-in|ease-out|ease-in-out|linear. The two systems align on duration band and deliberately not on curve.

rules.name: Stagger describes a list, or it is decoration
rules.body: The only staggered sequence in the app is ChartCard's expanded stat strip (three steps at 60/105/150ms) — a row of peers that genuinely appears as a row. Cap the total delay. Do not reinterpret scrolled sections, table rows, or card grids as staggered lists.

rules.name: The Measured-Floor Rule
rules.body: When a row of chips or badges repeats down a list, give each a minWidth taken from the measured widest real label, plus textAlign:center. Content-width chips vary on incidental things — "IMS · Starter" is wider than "IMS · Pro" — so the columns, and everything anchored after them, slide from row to row for no meaningful reason and the list reads ragged. Measure in the browser rather than guessing a number.

rules.name: space-between on two controls in a wide container is an anti-pattern
rules.body: It does not distribute, it banishes — the two items end up at opposite edges of however wide the container happens to be, with the entire remainder as dead space. Group related controls with a gap and let the container's own alignment place the group.

rules.name: No interactive control below 12px
rules.body: Chips and buttons in dense list rows sit at 12–12.5px with roughly 5–7px vertical padding; 10px is for genuinely non-interactive micro-labels only. 10px with 2px vertical padding is legible in a mockup, a squint in use, and a poor hit target.

rules.name: Never hand-roll a button's inline style when a variant exists
rules.body: The 2026-08-12 audit of ClientDrawer.js found six Danger Zone buttons each carrying a near-identical eight-property inline style object, with three different red alphas serving as an ad-hoc severity ladder, all at an off-scale 6px radius and none inheriting the hover transition. .btn-danger had existed the whole time. Drift concentrates almost perfectly in controls that opted out of a class — that is the single most reliable place to look for it.

rules.name: Every field needs id + htmlFor
rules.body: A label that is merely a sibling of its input, which is what .form-field renders by default, names nothing: screen readers announce an unnamed edit box and clicking the label focuses nothing. This is a systemic gap — 22 files use .form-field and only Login.js, ResetPassword.js and SelfServiceHome.jsx associate their labels — so treat it as the pattern to extend, and write new fields with the pair from the start.

rules.name: A control the user must reach cannot be display:none
rules.body: Hiding a real input behind a styled stand-in is fine; hiding it with display:none (or visibility:hidden) removes it from the tab order, so there is no keyboard path to it at all. Use the clip-based .visually-hidden utility when the input itself must stay reachable, or forward a real button's click to it.

rules.name: Any tab row needs real tablist semantics
rules.body: Not just buttons that look selected: role=tablist on the row, role=tab + aria-selected + aria-controls per tab, role=tabpanel + aria-labelledby on the body, and a roving tabIndex so the whole row is one stop in the page's tab order with the arrow keys (plus Home/End) moving inside it. Without the roving index, reaching the eighth tab by keyboard costs eight Tab presses — and the eighth tab is where the destructive actions live.

rules.name: The Text-vs-Fill Rule
rules.body: A signal colour used as TEXT takes the *-text variant; used as a FILL it takes the base token. One value cannot do both jobs on a light preset. Three exceptions, each found by applying the rule too broadly: a legend swatch keeps the series colour, a prop that receives a series colour keeps it, and a colour: inside a ternary is still a colour: — about half the real sites are ternaries a property-level regex silently skips.

rules.name: Rosé Dawn and Solarized were the floor, not Latte (history; Light is now the only light preset)
rules.body: History (all four light presets named here were retired in S607; Light is now the only light preset, so spot-check there). Failing signal-colour/surface combinations per light preset were: Rosé Dawn 10/10, Solarized 10/10, Bright 6/10, Latte 4/10, Warm Light 3/10. Spot-check colour work on Rosé Dawn, not on the preset that is easiest to recall.

rules.name: Never build a multi-series chart palette from the semantic tokens
rules.body: They are five roles, not five hues. accent and purple are the same hex on three of ten presets, which drew Food Cost and Labor Cost as one indistinguishable line on the chart whose entire purpose is telling them apart.

rules.name: Form controls do not inherit font-family, and must be told to
rules.body: Every browser substitutes its own UA default into input, button, select and textarea. One rule in index.css covers all four plus optgroup, which Firefox styles separately. Do not re-add per-class patches.

rules.name: A modal is a dialog or it is a trap
rules.body: role="dialog" + aria-modal + a labelled title, initial focus, a Tab trap, Escape, and focus restored to the trigger. A second modal implementation that skips these is only visually a modal: the page behind it stays fully focusable and Escape does nothing.

rules.name: Never .toISOString() a Date built from BS components
rules.body: bsToAd returns local midnight; at Nepal's UTC+05:45 .toISOString() lands at 18:15Z on the previous day, so slicing the first ten characters yields the wrong date for every user in the country. Use formatAd for a bare date string, bsDayBoundaryIso where the value meets a real timestamptz.

rules.name: A verdict colour on an unsettled figure is a lie
rules.body: A ratio whose numerator arrives in lumps and whose denominator accrues daily is arithmetic, not signal, early in a period. Render it neutral with an explicit "Day N of M · settles at month end" rather than painting it red and telling the reader to investigate immediately.

rules.name: Opacity is not de-emphasis on text
rules.body: It multiplies straight through the text colour — text2 at 0.45 measured well under AA. If a row is inactive, say so with a label; do not dim it.

rules.name: A paired token is only correct while it is actually measured
rules.body: --theme-accent-text was plain #ffffff on all five light presets of the time (four retired in S607) and failed on three of them: 2.84:1 on Rose Dawn, 3.61:1 on Light, 3.68:1 on Solarized — i.e. every .btn-primary in the product on those themes, for as long as they have existed. Fixed by giving those presets a dark hue-matched ink rather than darkening the accent, which also serves as a tint, border and dot where it was already correct. Reach for the token, then verify the token.

rules.name: A wrapper being new does not put the thing it wraps in scope
rules.body: ModuleGuideTab.jsx rendered its whole 'Watch out for' list in --theme-amber as body text — 2.05:1 on Rose Dawn (preset retired S607; the measurement is why the *-text variants exist), the worst measurement in the system — and survived because only its wrapper GuidesTab.jsx was in the changed-file set, so the hook never ran on it. When a critique or audit targets a page, include the components it composes, not just the files git reports (S594; the S521 stale-file lesson restated).

rules.name: A tier or add-on above the module set takes the accent plus a mark, not a fourth hue
rules.body: The admin client list carries IMS/HR/POS pills in accent/green/purple; Crest Suite Pro had none, and a fourth colour would have been exactly the One Accent Rule drift. It renders as ★ SUITE in the accent at a heavier fill (0.20 vs the modules' 0.10) and 700 weight — the glyph and the weight carry the distinction, the hue stays inside the system. A lapsed one greys to text3 rather than disappearing: an add-on that vanishes reads as one never bought.

rules.name: A <label> that names nothing is worse than no label
rules.body: The shape that survives every htmlFor sweep because it looks correct: a <label> over a button group, a read-only figure, or a repeating row's column is announced as a name the browser will never bind to a control. Those become a <span class="field-label"> with role="group"/"radiogroup" + aria-labelledby on the container and aria-pressed on the buttons. A <button> can never be named by a <label> at all, however adjacent.

rules.name: A <select> needs an accessible name even where the design gives it no visible caption
rules.body: Filter toolbars are the product's blind spot: 86 unnamed selects across 43 files — period pickers, category/status/vendor filters, sort orders — each announcing only its current option. aria-label where there is no visible text, id/htmlFor where there is. Inside a .map(), use a template aria-label naming the row, never a constant that repeats down the list.

rules.name: A standalone input takes .form-input; only a .form-field child is styled for free
rules.body: Until that class existed the only themed input rule was the descendant selector .form-field input, so an input in a plain flex row got no treatment and rendered as the browser's native white box — unmissable on dark presets, nearly invisible on light ones. The tell that the gap was real: sites that noticed either hand-copied all six declarations inline or borrowed .form-select, which carries cursor:pointer, so a text field announced itself as a menu.

rules.name: A native <input type="file"> is never shippable UI
rules.body: Its 'Choose File / No file chosen' chrome is drawn by the browser: no token reaches it, it ignores the type scale, and it renders in the OS language rather than the app's. The pattern is a .visually-hidden input (not display:none) with a real .btn forwarding the click.

rules.name: Use .panel-tab-bar for the row itself
rules.body: It carries display:flex + gap + flex-wrap + the bottom rule, so wrap behaviour is a property of the class rather than something each page has to remember. Seven IMS pages had hand-rolled the row inline; Stock Count's had seven tabs and no flexWrap — the exact shape that hid ClientDrawer's Danger tab.

rules.name: A report page must not show a number it has not computed
rules.body: The KPI strip does not render while loading or after a failure. Two report pages painted four stat cards ABOVE their own loading guard, so a multi-second fiscal-year read showed 'Capital in 90+ Day Stock: NPR 0' in green until the real number arrived, and on a failed read it stayed there. ReportPage gates stats/note/filters/footnote on !loading && !error; banners are not gated, because a period warning qualifies the page including its absence of data.

rules.name: A failed read is not an empty period
rules.body: 'Nothing to show' and 'could not load' are different facts and only one of them means the zeros on screen are real. Every read on two report pages destructured { data } and dropped error, then ran it through || [] — so an RLS rejection or a stalled token produced a complete, confident report of NPR 0. Strictly worse than a crash: a crash gets reported, a zero gets believed. firstError(results) is the one place a Promise.all batch is checked.

rules.name: The totals row and lining figures are the table's own, not the call site's
rules.body: .data-table tfoot had NO rule at all until S594, so every totals row in the product was hand-styled where it was written and three report pages built in one week produced three different treatments. font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums now sits on every .data-table td and .stat-value: Poppins' default figures are proportional, so a right-aligned currency column does not line up digit-for-digit.

rules.name: Never put role="button" on a <tr>
rules.body: The role overrides the row's implicit row role, taking it out of the table's structure — a screen reader stops associating that row's cells with their column headers, which on a table of currency columns is the entire content. The control belongs in a cell, as a real <button>: RowDisclosure (src/components/RowDisclosure.jsx) sets aria-expanded and stopPropagation()s so the row's own onClick cannot double-fire. This rule lived ONLY in this sidecar for months and was therefore copied forward into four tables; all four were fixed in S595 and the rule now also lives in DESIGN.md's prose, where someone reads it.

rules.name: A report that states a scope must state it everywhere the report goes
rules.body: Stock Ageing aged every fiscal year against new Date() while its selector accepted any past year, pushing every surviving batch into the 90+ band and reporting the whole stock value as stale — silently, in the alarming direction. It had no as-of date in the subtitle, the print title or the workbook, and its filter bar is no-print so a printed sheet showed a filtered table with no record of the filter. One scopeLine now feeds all four.

rules.name: The Signal Separation Rule
rules.body: Two signal colours that a reader compares must stay distinguishable *without hue*. Measured under deuteranopia (~6% of men) and protanopia (~2%), not by eye. Light's `redText`/`amberText` shipped at ΔE 3.2 — danger and warning were one colour for a red-green colour-blind reader — and were retuned in S608 to `#8f2440`/`#a85200`, the only pair of 120 searched that clears both axes while every variant holds ≥4.5:1. Where a band is a *scale* rather than a status (food cost healthy/watch/too-high), colour is not enough on its own at all: `fcBand()` also returns a `✓`/`△`/`▲` shape mark, distinguished by fill rather than hue, so the band survives greyscale and a monochrome print. A figure a person reads and acts on carries the mark; a chart axis or sparkline may take colour alone.

rules.name: The Signal Polarity Rule
rules.body: A signal colour is a **verdict**, so a figure compared against a target must be coloured by whether it moved in the *good* direction for that metric — not by which side of the line it landed on. Green and red are never neutral to an owner reading between services; there is no reading of a red ▼ that isn't "something went wrong here". The Daily Purchases vs Sales tooltip coloured both actual rows ▲ green / ▼ red literally, and reported live (S634) it painted `Purchases : NPR 2,295` against a NPR 3,112 target red — for running *under* the spending pace, which is the outcome you wanted. **Shape is the fact, colour is the verdict**: keep ▲/▼ literal so it agrees with the line the reader can see, and invert the colour per metric (`GOOD_DIRECTION` — sales `+1`, purchases `-1`). Applies wherever a cost sits beside a revenue: variance, budget-vs-actual, wastage, food-cost trend. Two consequences: shape stops being redundant with colour (a green ▼ and a red ▼ now both exist), so the magnitude must appear as **text** — the gap as a percentage of target, not a second currency figure — and any legend explaining the two series has to say the polarity out loud, because nothing else on screen admits that they are coloured by opposite conventions.

rules.name: The Chart Palette Rule
rules.body: Chart series come from the validated fixed-hex sets (`CHART_COLORS` / `VENDOR_SPLIT_COLORS`, `COST_BREAKDOWN_COLORS`), never the semantic tokens — and the sets themselves get re-measured whenever a slot moves. As shipped 2026-08-24/S609 the 8-series set is `#c9a84c #34d399 #60a5fa #f87171 #8b5cf6 #ea580c #22d3ee #f472b6`, worst pair ΔE 37.9 normal / 15.8 deuteranopia / 21.0 protanopia — all 28 pairs clear. It reached that only by moving two slots: blue and violet had sat at ΔE 0.4 under deuteranopia since the array was written, drawing two indistinguishable lines on any chart with five or more series. Two limits are accepted rather than hidden, and both rest on the same mitigation — these charts carry secondary encoding: paddingAngle gaps, on-slice percent labels, and name+value legends, so colour reinforces rather than carries. Tritanopia is not satisfied (worst pair ΔE 0.9); separating on the blue-yellow axis fights separating on red-green, and it is ~0.01% against ~8%. And the palette is tuned for the dark card — on Light, six of eight slots fall under the 3:1 non-text floor (worst `#22d3ee` at 1.81). Closing that means re-picking six hues that clear 3:1 on both surfaces *and* still separate under both red-green axes: a mid-tone set with a different character from today's vivid-on-charcoal one. That is a design decision, not a correction — do not make it silently while fixing something else.

rules.name: A page that renders into the body flow needs its own scrollport
rules.body: index.css sets `html, body { overflow-x: hidden }`, so body becomes its own scroll container sized to its content and a `position: sticky` child of the body has a scrollport that never scrolls. Every IMS/HR/POS screen is immune (the app shell scrolls its own div); the three pages that render into the body — guest menu, /login, /pricing — each had a sticky bar that had never once stuck, measured at 390x780 going top 0 to -250 to -600. Fix per page: `height: 100dvh; overflow-y: auto; overscroll-behavior: contain` on the page root, and delete any `min-height: 100vh` it carried, since 100vh >= 100dvh hands the scroll straight back to the body. Relaxing the shared rule was measured and rejected — it loses the guard entirely (1610px of overflow on a probe page). Invisible to review: it computes to sticky in devtools, and only getBoundingClientRect().top across real scroll positions catches it.

rules.name: Disabled and read-only: the surface carries the state, never the value
rules.body: Because `.form-field input` sets its own background, border and color, it overrode the UA's disabled styling — so until S603 a disabled field rendered identical to an editable one, on Sales and Overheads, the two pages where a locked period most needs to be obvious. The well flattens to transparent and the border steps to --theme-border-lt; the value's colour is left alone. Deliberately NOT `.btn:disabled`'s opacity 0.55 — a button's label is a verb you may not press, a field's content is data, and a locked period's figures must stay legible precisely because they can no longer be corrected. Two UA behaviours must be overridden explicitly or the treatment is defeated: WebKit paints disabled text with -webkit-text-fill-color, and iOS Safari layers its own opacity on top. An inline-styled control escapes all of it — that is what `disabledStyle()` in shared/inlineFieldState.js exists for.

rules.name: The 16px touch floor is a zoom trap, not a taste step
rules.body: Under @media (pointer: coarse) inputs go to 16px and bare buttons to a 44px minimum height. Below 16px iOS Safari zooms the viewport on focus and never zooms back, which on a product whose till and stock count are tablet surfaces turns 'enter the quantity' into 'now pan sideways to find Save'. Scoped to pointer type rather than a width breakpoint because the trigger is the input method, not the screen size. The rule carries `!important` and that is load-bearing: 370 controls across ~46 files set font-size inline, and no selector beats an inline style. The button half is `:not([class])` so it cannot silently re-decide the classed buttons that already have tuned values. It does not retire 'reach for a class' — a class also brings the [aria-invalid] hook, the :disabled treatment and the shape scale.

rules.name: The phone is a supported reporting surface
rules.body: `.stat-grid` is repeat(auto-fit, minmax(180px, 1fr)) and reflows on its own. Twenty-five report pages had overridden it inline with repeat(N, 1fr) up to N=6 — an inline style outranks every media query — so a phone rendered six crushed KPI columns on precisely the pages an owner checks between services. All removed; desktop is unchanged because auto-fit lands on the same count at desktop widths. Never pin a fixed column count on a KPI strip: if a row genuinely needs a different density, add a named variant in Layout.css that carries its own breakpoint.

rules.name: Report pages are one dialect, till screens are another
rules.body: A report is a report whichever module it belongs to — the person reading it is the same owner or accountant, arriving with the same expectations, often on the same afternoon. POS's four report pages had grown their own grammar (an inline-styled h2 where every other page opens with page-title, hand-rolled KPI tiles, a third tab family, mouse-only row drill-downs); that was drift, not a decision, and it is converged. The deliberate exception is the till: PosOrders and KitchenDisplay are position: fixed full-screen layers operated at arm's length on a busy floor, which is why their Modal usage needs its own zIndex. Do not converge those.

rules.name: A cell holding two things collapses first, and the auto layout decides that, not you
rules.body: table-layout is auto, so a column's width is bid for against its neighbours and a neighbour carrying white-space: nowrap always wins. The Purchases bill list is the reference case: its Item cell holds a name plus a category badge with a nowrap Vendor cell beside it, so a two-word name broke over two lines with the badge on a third and the row stood three lines tall to show one line of figures. The fix is nowrap on the cell, never a fixed width — .table-wrap's horizontal scroll exists to carry exactly this, and a width just moves the wrap somewhere else at the next screen size. Same failure with no second element at all: a Day cell holding 2026-08-17 collapses to its widest unbreakable fragment, 2026-, and breaks the date at every hyphen. Dates, codes, invoice refs and phone numbers all need nowrap for this reason.

rules.name: Row density is a table-level decision, made once
rules.body: The global td padding is 11px vertical. A table read as a dense ledger rather than a report of a dozen rows opts down through its own scoped class (table.purchases-table, 7px), never per cell — a per-cell inline padding is the shape that leaves one row taller than its neighbours the first time someone adds a column, and inline beats the class silently.

rules.name: Day columns say the month
rules.body: A Day column showing a bare 1 is legible only while the page header naming the month is on screen; print the sheet or read it back a month later and the number says nothing. Every period-scoped Day column renders formatBsDay(day, bsMonth) — '1st Bhadra' — and bsDayOrdinal(day) alone where the month is already stated beside it. Deliberately not the full-date form: this names a day inside the period already chosen, so it carries no year. Two behaviours are load-bearing: an absent or out-of-range month degrades to the bare ordinal rather than naming the wrong month, and day 0 (Sales' bulk sentinel) returns '' so each caller keeps its own dash. Excel exports keep the numeric column — text breaks a spreadsheet's sorting and filtering.

rules.name: Expanding a row shows detail in place, directly beneath it
rules.body: A `<tr className="detail-row">` with a full-width colSpan cell, never a panel appended after the table. Two cascade notes, both of which bit on the first implementation: `table.data-table tr:hover td` is a descendant selector, so without the .detail-row overrides in Layout.css hovering an expanded detail tints its own cell and every cell of any table nested inside it, lighting the whole panel up as one hoverable row. And if the parent row toggles the expansion on click, every control inside it must stopPropagation() or acting on the record also collapses the panel you were reading.

dos: Do use the theme's `accent-text` token as the foreground on any accent-colored background - it changes per preset and a hardcoded color will fail contrast on at least one of the two presets.
Do keep tonal alpha-tints (`table-hover`, `focus-ring`, badge backgrounds) at 2-18% opacity - enough to register as a state, never opaque enough to compete with real content.
Do wrap every wide table in the horizontal-scroll container rather than shrinking columns.
Do reserve the rationed 4th color (purple) for a genuine 4th/5th categorical need, not as a second accent.
Do put labels above form fields, always - never a placeholder standing in for a label.

Do give every status message a live region - `role="alert"` for errors, `role="status"` for confirmations. A message that is only *shown* announces nothing, and on a destructive surface that means no confirmation an action ran at all.
Do use the `*-text` variant whenever a signal colour is set as `color:` — and check the ternaries, which is where about half the real sites are.
Do keep a legend swatch identical to the series it labels, and let the adjacent label text carry the readable contrast.
Do give any modal the full dialog contract: role, `aria-modal`, a labelled title, initial focus, a Tab trap, Escape, and focus restored to the trigger.
Do disclose an estimate where it is read, inline and visible, not in a hover tooltip — a figure carrying a red/amber/green verdict has to say what it is built from.
Do render a report's could-not-load state as its own thing, never as the empty state, and never above a KPI strip that is still showing zeros (added 2026-08-19/S594 — see Report shell).

Do put a validation message under the box it names, with `aria-invalid` on the control and `aria-describedby` pointing at the message — one string for the whole form tells a screen-reader user that a save failed and never which control to fix (added 2026-08-23/S603 — see Inputs / Fields).
donts: Don't build dense, hierarchy-less layouts in the name of "fitting more in" - that's the legacy-ERP failure mode this product is explicitly positioned against.
Don't reach for purple gradients, Inter-everywhere, or a templated hero-plus-three-cards layout - the generic-AI-SaaS look PRODUCT.md names directly as an anti-reference.

Don't invent a stronger/different shadow to mean "important" or "premium." Card elevation (`--theme-card-shadow`) is now uniform policy across every card, not a decoration budget to spend more of - the floating-action and live-pulse shadows are the only two that still carry extra meaning (see Elevation).
Don't hardcode white or black as text on an accent background - use the paired `accent-text` token.

Don't use a second saturated brand color alongside Aged Brass on the same screen; if a fourth category is genuinely needed, that's what the rationed purple token is for. (No exceptions remain; Bright's colorful KPI badges were the only named one, retired with that preset in S607.)

Don't build a multi-series chart palette from the semantic tokens — they are five *roles*, not five validated hues, and nothing measures them as a series set. Both earlier justifications have now expired (accent/purple being one hex died with those presets in S607; Light's `red`/`amber` ΔE 3.1 was fixed in S608), which is itself the argument: the tokens move for reasons that have nothing to do with series separation. Use the validated fixed-hex sets (`CHART_COLORS`, `COST_BREAKDOWN_COLORS`) and re-measure when you touch them — S608 found `CHART_COLORS` slots 3 and 5 at ΔE 0.4 under deuteranopia, i.e. two identical lines on any chart with five or more series, and nobody had noticed.
Don't dim a row with `opacity` to de-emphasise it; opacity multiplies through the text colour and takes it below AA. Label the state instead.

Don't put `role="button"` on a `<tr>`. It removes the row from the table's structure, so the cells stop being associated with their column headers. Put a real `<button>` in the first cell (see Data Tables).
Don't paint a verdict colour on a figure that has not settled yet — early in a period a lumpy-numerator ratio is arithmetic, not signal.
Don't let a page compute a number it then shows before the read has returned. A KPI painted during load is a claim the page cannot yet support, and on a green token it reads as a healthy one.
Don't signal a failing field with colour alone, and don't give it a styling hook separate from `aria-invalid` — the two drift, and a form that looks validated then reads as unlabelled.

Don't put a `position: sticky` element in the body flow and assume it sticks — `index.css`'s `html, body { overflow-x: hidden }` makes body its own scrollport, and it had silently killed three of them. Give the page root its own scroll container and measure it (see Layout).

Don't dim a disabled *field* the way a disabled button is dimmed. A button's label is a verb; a field's content is data, and a locked period's figures have to stay legible precisely because they can no longer be corrected — flatten the surface instead (see Inputs / Fields).
